pass_a_gloss: What need is there for the silence of the many and often, also to me most of all now, and being forced to be silent and to speak both willingly and unwillingly. For I have neglected in such a way the good and fine words, which are spoken or written by the chosen and approved men with uninterrupted sequence, using names and verbs in order. It is a truly Greek work to have practiced this charm. But now eight years have passed for me, since which I have not spoken or written anything great or small, nor have I heard from another who writes or speaks privately or publicly in panegyric and competitive speeches, except for those wonderful men who have practiced the good philosophy, to whom elegance and simplicity of names are of less concern. They, placing their voices second, wish to examine and proclaim the matters themselves with precision. I think they do not wish to, but rather they wish very much to pour out the good and precise thoughts, but perhaps they are unable to do so because they have the sacred and divine word in their minds, and the word that is in their speeches is elegant, and each of the two men has his own excesses, and it is difficult to encompass in a single and the same, and this small and human soul, being things most opposite. If thought and discovery are somehow friends and co-workers, then silence is a friend. But the eloquent man, you will not find anywhere else, except in voices and the continuous practice of them. And indeed, the mind also learns something else very much, and the mouth is bound by the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even small, to the voice of the Greeks, our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all men under the human rule, not being careless or learning superficially, being themselves accurate and varied and wonderful, and being called most Greek, expressed and handed down in the Roman language, which is persuasive and boastful and adapted to the royal authority, but burdensome to me. But in no other way is it possible or desirable for me. Since, however, our words are like certain images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters and skilled craftsmen, who use not only similar but also varied and very beautiful colors to paint their paintings, without being hindered in any way, we would agree.

pass_b_english: I've been forced into silence, and it's a strange feeling, especially for me, now more than ever. The truth is, I've neglected the art of using beautiful and elegant words, a skill that's highly valued in Greek culture. It's a charm that's uniquely Greek, and one that I've failed to practice in the last eight years. During this time, I haven't spoken or written anything of significance, nor have I heard anyone else do so, except for a few remarkable individuals who have dedicated themselves to the pursuit of philosophy. These men are not concerned with the elegance of their language, but rather with the precision and accuracy of their thoughts. They believe that the true power of language lies not in the words themselves, but in the ideas and concepts they convey. As a result, they focus on examining and proclaiming the truth, rather than on crafting beautiful speeches. I think they're driven by a desire to share their knowledge and insights with others, but they may be limited by their own abilities and the complexity of the ideas they're trying to express. If thinking and discovery are closely tied, then silence can be a powerful tool for learning and growth. However, eloquence is a different matter altogether, and it can only be developed through practice and dedication. The mind is capable of learning and absorbing new ideas, but the mouth is limited by the words it can speak. I wish I could express myself in a way that would do justice to the Greek language, which is so highly valued by our leaders, who have adopted the Roman tongue as their own. They use it to persuade and impress, but to me, it feels like a burden. Perhaps it's because I'm not used to it, or maybe it's just not my style. Either way, I know that words are like images that reflect the depths of our souls, and that those who are skilled in the art of language can use it to create beautiful and lasting works, just like a painter uses colors to create a masterpiece. And so, I acknowledge the power of language and the importance of using it well, even if it doesn't come naturally to me.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant interpretive additions and shifts in agency/meaning not present in the Greek or Pass A. Specifically, Pass B adds 'it's a strange feeling' and 'a skill that's highly valued in Greek culture' which are not in the source. It also adds 'They believe that the true power of language lies not in the words themselves, but in the ideas and concepts they convey' and 'they focus on examining and proclaiming the truth, rather than on crafting beautiful speeches', which are paraphrases/interpretations rather than translations. Most critically, Pass B misrepresents the Greek regarding the Roman language: the Greek says the Greeks were 'handed down to the Roman voice/language' (παραδοϑέντες τῇ Ῥωμαίων φωνῇ), whereas Pass B claims 'our leaders, who have adopted the Roman tongue as their own', which changes the historical/linguistic context of the argument. Pass B also adds 'Perhaps it's because I'm not used to it, or maybe it's just not my style', which is entirely absent from the Greek.
reasons: Pass B adds significant non-textual commentary and interpretive filler: 'it's a strange feeling', 'a skill that's highly valued in Greek culture', 'They believe that the true power of language lies not in the words themselves...', 'Perhaps it's because I'm not used to it, or maybe it's just not my style'.

Pass B misrepresents the clause 'παραδοϑέντες τῇ Ῥωμαίων φωνῇ' (handed down to the Roman voice/language) by stating 'our leaders, who have adopted the Roman tongue as their own', which is an interpretive expansion not found in the Greek.
